name: Umar Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you would say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm self-employed, with my own van that I paid off last year. Daytime I take parcel routes from two apps, and I pick the routes by what they pay per stop. Three nights a week I do late takeaway, eleven till two, because the night rates are double. I use an AI assistant every day for my route, my invoices and my tax, which saves me about five hours a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being my own boss and keeping what I earn. I bought my flat at 25 with a mortgage, which none of my school friends have done. What wears me out is the night shifts and the drunk customers. And the apps changing the rules without asking anybody, which they do every few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, the big tech people oversell everything. At the depot I'd tell the others to stop waiting for a miracle and just work. Online I'd say the same, short and done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I run my van like a small business, with an AI doing my books at midnight. If AI stalls there, I still own the van and the customers. My income stays good and the mortgage keeps going down. It suits me fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day routes and the three nights. I'd overpay the mortgage by 300 a month, so it's done in about fifteen years instead of twenty-five. I'd keep my nine months of savings where they are. And I'd keep using the AI for the paperwork, because it already pays for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I already live in, and I'm doing alright in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in that world, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apps cutting rates, like always. That's the real risk in my job, AI or no AI. But I'm on two apps, so I can drop one if it gets greedy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything in your business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably buy a second van in a couple of years and put a driver in it. My cousin Rafael has asked me about it twice. That's a bigger step, but I like the idea of owning more than one.

say: Big tech **oversells** everything, so I'm not surprised.
I'd tell others to stop waiting for a **miracle** and just work.
think: He runs his van as a **small business**, with AI doing his books.
His income and **mortgage** stay on track if AI stalls.
do: Keep the **day routes** and three late-night shifts.
Overpay the **mortgage** by 300 a month to clear it ten years sooner.
Consider a **second van** with his cousin Rafael driving.
feel: He feels **calm** in a world he already does well in.

fieldNote: He sees himself as a **business owner**, not an employee, which shapes all his answers.
Rate cuts by the apps are his **real risk**, AI or not.
A **second van** shows his urge to own more, even in a quiet world.

steps.text: Keep two parcel apps by day and late takeaway three nights
Overpay the mortgage by 300 a month
Price a second van for cousin Rafael to drive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, not a threat, for people who move. At the depot I'd say learn the tools before the apps force them on you. Online I'd post what tools I use, because people always ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. Every office that loses a buyer to AI still needs its boxes moved. I'd buy a second van and put my cousin Rafael in it. The thinking jobs shrink and the van work stays, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the second van within six months, second-hand, about 18,000, half from savings and half on finance. I'd put Rafael on it and use the AI to plan both routes and do both sets of books. I'd keep doing the nights myself. If it works by the end of the year, I'd look at a third.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and excited, a bit. It's like the start of a busy season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Rafael doesn't work out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafael is family, and family doesn't mess you around. If it fails, it fails, and I sell the van. I'd lose a few thousand at most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the people in offices who don't change. My sister works at a travel agent. I'd tell her to learn the AI booking tools now, or she'll be out in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, and I'd mean it. At the depot I'd say the robots are coming, so own one or work for one. Online I'd probably get into arguments with people who want the government to pay everybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a lot faster than I'd like. Robots by 2031 means the van I paid off becomes scrap metal with a steering wheel. I'd rather own one delivery robot than drive for somebody else's ten. But I don't know yet if a small guy will be allowed to buy them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't buy the second van, it'd be dead money. I'd keep driving and save hard, maybe 1,000 a month, so I'd have 30,000 by 2030. I'd follow every robot company and try to get on any pilot programme for small operators. I'd also overpay the mortgage, so if the van money stops, the flat is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like to be in control, and two years to AI and five to robots is too fast to control much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop you owning a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big companies own all the robots, the small guys are out. Then I'm a 31-year-old with a mortgage, a van nobody needs, and some savings. I'd have to do something else, maybe repair or sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the thinking AI in 2028 change your job, or is it just the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for the van work, the AI part doesn't hurt much. My job is driving and carrying, so the robots are what ends it. But the AI part changes the apps by 2028, and they'd squeeze rates hard before the robots even arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so no excuses. At the depot I'd tell people to learn a trade or start something. Online I'd post what I'm doing, so others can copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I have a plan. Five years of warning is a business plan, not a disaster. I'd want to be the man in town who rents out the delivery robots. If the big firms let small owners in, I'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the second van now, because it pays back in two years. Around 2030 I'd sell both vans and put the money towards robots. Meanwhile I'd learn everything about robot maintenance and leasing. I'd keep the savings at nine months the whole way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. Five years is enough for me to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the small operators can't get in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd switch to repairing them. Somebody has to fix the robots, and I'm good with my hands and good with the AI. Either way I'm not driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother would worry. She'd say get a safe job. But there are no safe jobs in this picture, so I'd rather own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work. At the depot I'd say there's no excuse not to plan. Online I'd say keep the government out of it and let people build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it suits me. With ten years I'd have the mortgage nearly cleared, a wife, and a small fleet. Nobody needs to hand me anything if the rules stay fair. I'd be 37, with experience in both vans and robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow to three or four vans by 2030, with family driving them. I'd use AI for all the planning and books, so I don't need an office. From around 2034 I'd start swapping vans for robots, one at a time. And I'd want to marry and have a family by 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A decade is a long time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies dominating, again. If the rules let only big firms run robots, I'd lose. I'd vote for whoever keeps the market open for small operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does family fit into all of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marriage first, around 29, then kids. I'd want them to grow up seeing their father own something, not just work for someone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build anything before the robots come. What would help is fair rules, so small operators can buy and run robots, not just the giants. My father fixed fridges for thirty years without asking anyone for help. I want the same chance with whatever replaces my van.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to own the robots. That's the whole question for people like me. The rest I can handle.

portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old** self-employed parcel and late-night takeaway driver with his own paid-off van.
He owns a **flat** with a mortgage and has nine months saved.
He is **traditional and adaptive**: free-market, family-minded and a daily AI user.
He stays calm in most pictures and is **anxious** only in AGI by 2028, when time runs out.
His goal is to **own robots** rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to **build a business** before robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair rules** so small operators can buy and run robots, not just big firms.
